anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Optimizer Statistics Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to process more rows, columns, or time than the business case requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Tables, indexes, partitions, and constraints are structured in a way that does not support the workload’s access patterns, pushing even well-written statements toward inefficient data access.
Optimizer Statistics Anomaly : Row-count, histogram, or correlation metadata is stale or absent, causing the optimizer to mis-estimate cardinalities and choose sub-optimal plans.

When all three conditions coexist, the database exhibits extreme and erratic latency spikes, runaway I/O, and CPU saturation. Queries already bloated by poor SQL logic devolve into repeated full-table or non-covering index scans because useful indexes are missing or mis-designed; simultaneously, outdated statistics convince the optimizer that these heavy plans are cheap, so it avoids better alternatives or fails to consider them. Symptoms include: the same statements dominating slow-query and lock-wait logs, sudden plan regressions after data changes, high variance between estimated and actual rows, excessive temp-space usage from mis-sized hash or sort operations, lock escalation due to long-running transactions, and dramatic performance improvements only when all three layers (SQL, schema, and statistics) are corrected together.

Causally, ill-formed SQL amplifies pressure on the physical design: wide scans and Cartesian joins become catastrophic when no suitable indexes exist. The deficient physical design, in turn, inflates the cost of every superfluous access the workload demands. Stale or inaccurate statistics mask these deficiencies from the optimizer, preventing it from selecting whatever limited indexing aids do exist and discouraging DBAs from recognizing design gaps, because estimated costs appear acceptable. Each layer therefore reinforces the others: bad SQL drives demand, bad design blocks efficient supply, and bad statistics obstruct corrective planning, jointly degrading both OLTP responsiveness and OLAP throughput.

entry.official_description: A %-.192s must include all columns in the table's partitioning function (prefixed columns are not considered).
entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
